learn.title: We've launched OpenTelemetry export in beta, so you can trace Messages API requests and Claude Managed Agents sessions in your observability backend.
learn.headline: Claude API adds OpenTelemetry tracing export in beta for Messages and agent sessions
learn.reason: Lets you trace token use and latency across agent loops, which is your next topic.

card.headline: Claude API and SDK can now export OpenTelemetry traces, in beta
card.term_meaning: A trace is the full record of one request as it moves through your system. A span is one step inside it, such as one model call or one tool use.
card.why_it_matters: When an LLM app is slow or wrong, you need to see which step failed. Now Claude requests and tool uses show up as spans in the observability tool you already use (a tool that collects logs and traces). You can also track token spend and latency, and build evals (tests of model output) from real traffic.
card.example: A tool-runner request shows up as an answer_question span. Inside it are a Messages client span, a web search tool step run by the API, a custom get_weather tool span, and a second request with the tool result. Each step has its own timing and token counts. It is like a pipeline run log where every task has its own duration.
card.say_it: Tracing records each model call and tool call as a span inside one trace, so I can debug slow or failed LLM requests and measure token cost per step.
card.follow_up_why: Because an agent makes many model and tool calls per user request, and without a span for each one I can't tell which step was slow, expensive or wrong.
card.reality_check: This is the maker's own docs, and the feature is in beta. The docs list partners such as Langfuse and Grafana Cloud. The source doesn't say what it costs. Adding an API destination needs Console Admin permission, which a free-plan user may not have. SDK tracing needs no special permission.
card.try_it: Read the SDK tracing setup page. Then point a local Langfuse or any OTLP (OpenTelemetry's wire format) receiver at it, if you have an SDK key. If you have no key, just read the span names.

learn.title: v2.1.299
learn.headline: Claude Code compacts idle 200K+ token chats before the one-hour prompt cache expires
learn.reason: Shows prompt caching and context cost in practice; directly on your agent-cost path.

card.headline: Claude Code 2.1.299 compacts idle long chats before the prompt cache expires
card.term_meaning: Prompt caching lets the provider reuse work on a long prompt you already sent, so repeats are faster and cheaper. Compaction shrinks a long conversation into a summary so it takes less context.
card.why_it_matters: The cache here lasts one hour. If you leave a chat idle past that, your next message makes the model reprocess the whole history. Idle compaction shrinks the chat first, so you spend less of your plan's usage. It also shows how context size, cache expiry and cost are linked in agent loops.
card.example: A conversation of 200K+ tokens left idle for about 54 minutes is compacted before the one-hour cache expires. Your next message then doesn't reprocess everything. You can change the 200K minimum with CLAUDE_CODE_IDLE_COMPACT_MIN_TOKENS, or turn it off with "idleCompaction": false in settings.json. Both need v2.1.290 or later.
card.say_it: Prompt caching reuses an already-processed prefix until it expires, so compacting a long idle conversation before expiry avoids paying to reprocess all of it.
card.follow_up_why: Because the cost and latency of a turn grow with the number of input tokens, and an expired cache means the full history is processed again.
card.reality_check: This is from the release notes only. The source gives no measured savings. You can try it today because it is in the Claude Code you already use, but it only applies to 200K+ token conversations.
card.try_it: Run claude update. Then check that your Claude Code version is 2.1.299 or later. Look at settings.json to see where "idleCompaction" would go.

learn.title: v0.40.4
learn.headline: Ollama adds one-line yes/no and classification from the terminal, and MLX on Apple silicon
learn.reason: Free local classification and faster Apple silicon runs fit your 24 GB Mac.

card.headline: Ollama 0.40.4 adds a command-line way to ask yes/no or label questions
card.term_meaning: The source doesn't define it. From the examples, it is a model used to answer yes/no questions, pick a label for text, or score text against a rubric (a scoring guide).
card.why_it_matters: Classifying text and scoring it are common eval and pipeline jobs. Now you can do them from the terminal with a local model, for free. The release says decision models are supported by the MLX runner on Apple silicon, so they fit your Mac.
card.example: The release shows: ollama run nimble --ask "Is a refund being requested?" < ticket.txt. It feeds one support ticket in and asks a yes/no question. It is like a quick classification step in a batch job, but you write no code.
card.say_it: A decision model is built to give a yes/no, a label or a score instead of free text, which suits classification and grading tasks.
card.follow_up_why: Because many pipeline steps need a constrained answer, and a model that gives only a label is easier to run in bulk and to check than free-form text.
card.reality_check: This is the maker's release note, with no benchmarks. The source doesn't say how big the nimble model is or how accurate it is. You can try it free with Ollama on your Mac, but check the model's size first.
card.try_it: Update Ollama to 0.40.4. Put a short sample ticket in ticket.txt. Run the command from the release note and see whether the answer is a clean yes/no.

learn.title: Run fast, private agents on-device with LFM2.5-24B-A2B
learn.headline: Liquid AI's 24B-parameter LFM2.5 model runs on-device for tool-using agents
learn.reason: Fits your 24 GB Mac and is built for tool calls, so you can practise agent loops locally.

card.headline: Liquid AI publishes LFM2.5-24B-A2B, pitched for fast, private on-device agents
card.term: mixture of experts (inferred from the name)
card.term_meaning: The source doesn't explain the name. "24B-A2B" usually means 24 billion total parameters with about 2 billion active per token. That is a mixture of experts design, where only some of the model's parts run for each token.
card.why_it_matters: If the name means that, then speed would be closer to a 2B model, but memory use would still be that of a 24B model. That matters on a 24 GB Mac. Whether it fits depends on the file size, and the source doesn't say.
card.example: The page lists three 24B text-generation models. Their downloads are 4.07k, 73 and 2.88k. The text we have has no benchmarks, file sizes or memory needs, so it gives no real numbers for how it would run on your Mac.
card.say_it: A 24B-A2B model has 24B total parameters but about 2B active per token, so it is cheaper to run per token but still needs memory for all the weights.
card.follow_up_why: Because all experts must be loaded in memory so the router can pick any of them, while only the chosen few do compute for each token.
card.reality_check: Only the maker's blog title is shown, and the page text is mostly empty. The source gives no benchmarks, sizes or license, and the reading of the name is my inference. Check the model card before downloading, because a 24B model may be too big for 24 GB unless it is quantized (stored in smaller numbers).
card.try_it: Open the Hugging Face page and read the model card. Check the quantized file sizes, and only pull one that is well under 24 GB.

learn.title: google/embeddinggemma-2: new open feature-extraction model (0.7B parameters, about 0 GB of memory at 4-bit)
learn.headline: Google releases EmbeddingGemma 2, a small open embedding model under Apache 2.0
learn.reason: Small embedding model that runs locally; directly relevant to RAG and embeddings interviews.

card.headline: Google released embeddinggemma-2, a small open model that turns text into number vectors.
card.term_meaning: An embedding model turns a piece of text into a list of numbers (a vector). Texts with similar meaning get vectors that sit close together.
card.why_it_matters: Embeddings are the search part of RAG (retrieval-augmented generation: fetch relevant text, then give it to an LLM). A 0.7B model is small enough to run locally on your 24 GB Mac with no API key and no cost. The licence is apache-2.0, which allows free use.
card.example: The source lists 0.7B parameters and the apache-2.0 licence. Think of it like building a lookup key for each document chunk, as you would index a SQL column. You embed every chunk once, store the vectors, then embed a user question and find the nearest chunks.
card.say_it: An embedding model maps text to vectors so that similar meanings are close, which lets a RAG system find relevant chunks by distance instead of exact keywords.
card.follow_up_why: Because keyword search misses paraphrases, while vectors capture meaning, so a question worded differently can still match the right document.
card.reality_check: The source is only a model listing: it gives no benchmark results, and its '0 GB at 4-bit' memory figure looks like a rounding error, so don't trust it. At 0.7B parameters it should be light enough for a 24 GB Mac, but the source doesn't say how well it works.
card.try_it: Check whether Ollama or Hugging Face has the model (huggingface.co/google/embeddinggemma-2). Embed 10 short sentences and compare cosine similarity (a score of how close two vectors are) for a paraphrase pair versus an unrelated pair.
